Staging environment for tomorrow’s demo

standup.text:
Payments and platform engineering standup

We reviewed the payments retry fix, orders migration, search ranker, and auth refactor. Staging identity-provider configuration is blocking the auth rollout, while the Kubernetes upgrade date still needs confirmation.

## Action items
- [ ] Finish the webhook retry dashboard panel by end of tomorrow (me)
- [ ] Investigate whether the SDK update caused Jen’s feature-flag evaluation latency increase (me)
- [ ] Send Priya the audience configuration notes from the billing service today (me)
- [ ] Confirm the Kubernetes upgrade date in the channel (me)
- [ ] Finish the orders migration rollback path by Thursday (Tomasz)
- [ ] Gather at least another week of search ranker traffic before reporting results to product (Jen)
- [ ] Paste the platform ticket for the staging identity-provider blocker in the channel after standup (Priya)

## My update
- The payments webhook retry fix is merged.
  - Callbacks previously retried indefinitely on 4xx responses; they now back off and stop after five retries.
- The dashboard panel remains unfinished, with an estimated half-day to one day of work.

## Tomasz
- The orders table migration ran against the full staging copy in about 40 minutes, with no observed locks.
- The rollback path is half-written; certificate-renewal work interrupted progress.
- The Kubernetes upgrade may have moved to the 20th because of the freeze.

## Jen
- The new search ranker entered shadow mode on Monday.
  - Click-through is up roughly 0.4%, but the change is within noise and is not yet considered a win.
- Shadow traffic is showing a possible eight-millisecond p99 increase in feature-flag evaluation latency.
  - I suspect the SDK version I updated last week may be responsible.

## Priya
- The session-token auth refactor is basically done, with everything moved off the old cookie helper.
- The staging identity provider cannot issue tokens with the new audience claim.
  - This blocks staging verification, which is required to sign off on the production rollout.
  - A PLAT ticket is open; the platform team said they would investigate, but timing is unclear because they are swamped.
- The billing service previously had a similar audience issue.
  - I think the fix was to add the audience to the identity provider’s allowed list.

## Open questions
- When will the platform team resolve the staging identity-provider blocker: today, next week, or later?

hiring.text:
Rahul Venkataraman interview debrief

We reviewed Rahul Venkataraman’s four rounds for the senior backend role. Strong system design and positive motivation signals outweighed mixed coding feedback enough to move forward to reference checks, with team dynamics needing further investigation.

## Action items
- [ ] Contact the recruiter today to request references from two former managers and one peer (me).
- [ ] Ask references about Rahul’s role in team attrition, how he worked with teammates, whether they would work with him again, and how he handles losing technical arguments (me).
- [ ] Send the debrief summary after the meeting (me).

## System design — Priya
- Strong hire signal: Rahul proactively asked about write volume and proposed an event-store partitioning scheme.
  - His rebalance answer covered backpressure and idempotent consumers without prompting.
- He was clear about gaps in his experience.
  - He had not run the proposed broker in production and wanted to verify failover semantics before committing to it; Priya viewed this positively.

## First coding round — Dmitri
- Leaning no hire, but not a hard no.
- Rahul completed interval merge, but spent roughly ten minutes on an incorrect approach before correcting it.
  - Dmitri appreciated his thinking aloud.
- He did not finish concurrent cache eviction.
  - The structure and locking were mostly right, but he ran out of time and struggled to explain a race condition.

## Second coding round — Imani
- Lean hire: Rahul completed both problems with clean code and wrote tests without prompting.
- Scoping remained a concern because he asked few clarifying questions on the second problem.
  - He handled the edge case Imani intended to probe, but she remained uncertain about his approach to identifying requirements.

## Hiring manager chat — Lena
- Positive culture and motivation signals: Rahul was thoughtful and specific about wanting to leave.
  - He has spent two years maintaining a monolith and wants to build new things; money was not his stated motivation.
- He spoke candidly about losing a rewrite disagreement with his previous manager.
  - He accepted the outcome but said he would have pushed harder on one aspect.
- Rahul briefly implied he may have contributed to attrition on his previous team, then moved on.
  - Lena did not have time to explore whether this was humility or a substantive concern; Priya’s technical round provided no additional team-dynamics evidence.

## Next-stage assessment
- Decided: Move forward to reference checks.
  - Imani’s coding result helped balance Dmitri’s concerns; the attrition concern warranted targeted follow-up rather than stopping the process.

## Open questions
- Did Rahul contribute to his previous team’s attrition, or was his comment self-effacing?
- How consistently does he scope requirements and handle concurrency problems?

oneonone.text:
Ingestion redesign and career growth

Daniela and I discussed moving toward design ownership and cross-team leadership, with an ingestion redesign proposal as a possible next step. We also agreed to sharpen the billing postmortem and update the rollback runbook; the proposal is the priority.

## Action items
- [ ] Draft an ingestion redesign one-pager for Daniela by this Friday, covering the problem, a couple of options, and a rough estimate; flag unknowns and let her know if it slips to Monday (me)
- [ ] Give the alerting gap its own section in the billing postmortem and sharpen the contributing factors (me)
- [ ] Add the outdated rollback runbook to the postmortem as an action item owned by me, and update it; tentatively by the end of next week, with timing flexible because it is less urgent than the proposal (me)
- [ ] Ask Joaquin for ingestion cluster throughput metrics and dashboard context, mentioning Daniela approved twenty minutes of his time (me)
- [ ] Loop me into the context on Priya’s downstream-consumer work and consider potential overlap with the ingestion redesign (Daniela)
- [ ] Decide who else should see the proposal after reviewing it (Daniela)

## Design ownership and staff track
- I feel like I’m treading water after roughly eight months of integrations, bug fixes, and occasional migrations; I want to design systems, not just implement others’ designs.
- I’m interested in both architecture and technical leadership, including owning a design doc end to end.
  - Daniela said my retry-logic design doc last spring was clean, and Marcus had highlighted it in review.
- Owning something by Q3 felt doable; I suggested the long-backlogged event ingestion redesign.
  - Daniela cautioned that one version could overlap with Priya’s downstream-consumer work and create cross-team friction without context.
- The staff track remains a possibility, not a promise.
  - Daniela said successful ingestion work and demonstrated cross-team scope would be meaningful signals, framing this as an opportunity rather than a test.

## Ingestion proposal
- Decided: Start with a one-page proposal rather than a full design doc, with Daniela as the initial audience.
- Write it so Marcus can understand it without prior context, since he will probably ask about it.
- Rough estimates are acceptable; distinguish known information from gaps.
  - I don’t have exact current throughput figures. Joaquin has the ingestion cluster dashboards and likely set up most of them.
- Full ownership and scope of the redesign remain parked pending more context.

## Billing rollout and postmortem
- The billing service rollout shipped Tuesday and was mostly smooth.
  - A smaller recurrence of the cache issue was caught in staging, showing the value of the earlier postmortem work.
- Daniela thought the root cause section was good, but contributing factors needed more emphasis.
  - Alerts did not fire for forty minutes, which she called the most actionable fact in the document.
  - I had hesitated because the on-call setup is Dev’s area; Daniela emphasized that the goal is preventing incidents, not protecting appearances.
- The rollback runbook was out of date and mentioned only in a comment, not the document.

## Next check-in
- Decided: Meet again at the same time next week.

## Open questions
- What ingestion redesign scope would avoid overlap with Priya’s team?
- Will the proposal lead to end-to-end design ownership and the cross-team scope needed for progress toward the staff track?

sales.text:
Harbor Freight Logistics Lintly pilot

We explored Lintly for Harbor Freight Logistics’ slow, noisy code reviews and outlined a six-week platform-team pilot. The kickoff remains tentative pending platform-team confirmation, security approval and pilot pricing; SOC 2 Type II requirements may block SaaS deployment.

## Action items

- [ ] Send the SOC 2 Type I report and penetration test summary today (me)
- [ ] Check with compliance about an auditor bridge letter and follow up by Thursday (me)
- [ ] Confirm whether Enterprise on-prem scoping is worth pursuing (me)
- [ ] Put a tentative hold on the seventh for pilot kickoff (me)
- [ ] Add the pre-commit hook to the pilot setup document (me)
- [ ] Send a Business tier quote for 39 active seats (me)
- [ ] Seek manager approval for a pilot rate and return with a number before Thursday (me)
- [ ] Send the follow-up email within the next hour (me)
- [ ] Confirm the seventh and the pilot group with the platform lead (Marcus)
- [ ] Take the security questions to legal, including the Type II requirement and whether a bridge letter is acceptable (Marcus)

## Current workflow and needs

- Harbor Freight Logistics has roughly 45 engineers across platform, routing and contractors.
  - Six are contractors; two are leaving at month-end. I estimated probably 39 active seats, depending on churn.
- Reviews stall on style, naming, unused imports and missed error handling rather than substantive logic.
  - Median time to first review is about three days, followed by another one or two days of back-and-forth.
- Previous linters were disabled because of noise, including roughly 900 warnings on day one.
- CI is mostly Jenkins, with frequent timeouts; the mobile driver app team uses some GitHub Actions.
  - Lintly supports both, so consolidation is not required before starting.
- Lintly baselines and suppresses existing findings, surfaces only new PR issues under team-selected rules, and ranks findings by severity.
  - Warn-only mode annotates without blocking merges.

## Pilot scope and timing

- Marcus proposed a six-week platform-team pilot with eight to ten people.
- Decided: Start in warn-only mode for at least the first two weeks.
  - Security-only blocking afterward was floated, not finalized.
- Decided: Include the optional pre-commit hook in pilot scope.
  - Secret scanning catches common credential patterns and high-entropy strings. Without the hook, it can block PR merges but not local commits.
  - It complements rather than replaces a secrets vault or GitHub push protection.
- Decided: Treat the first week as setup and exclude it from adoption metrics.
- Success criteria would be defined together, with review cycle time the VP’s priority.
  - Other proposed measures were style-related review comments and developer sentiment.
  - I proposed baselining Jenkins and GitHub data during the first week.
- Setup by the twenty-eighth was initially possible if paperwork moved this week; the seventh became the tentative kickoff because of the first-week release freeze.
  - Marcus thinks the freeze covers production deployments only, but engineers may be too busy for strong adoption that week.

## Security and deployment

- Okta SSO is non-negotiable; Business and above support SAML and SCIM for automatic provisioning and deprovisioning.
  - Business also includes audit logs exportable to their SIEM.
- Lintly analyzes source code in memory and retains findings metadata, not source code.
  - Customer code is not used for model training; this is covered in the terms and DPA.
- Lintly received SOC 2 Type I in March.
  - The Type II observation window runs through the end of Q3, with the report expected in October.
- Procurement requires Type II for vendors with source-code access.
  - Whether a current Type I report plus a bridge letter is acceptable needs legal confirmation.
- On-prem deployment is Enterprise-only and usually requires a few weeks of setup with the solutions team.
  - Keeping code inside their VPC could potentially clear the concern; SaaS-only may be blocked by legal.
- Decided: Explore on-prem feasibility in parallel with the Type I documentation review.

## Pricing and commercial terms

- Pricing is per active developer seat per month.
  - Active means opening or commenting on a PR within the last 30 days; rolled-off contractors are not counted.
- Team costs $22 per seat per month, billed annually, including core rules, Jenkins and GitHub Actions integrations, and standard support.
- Business costs $38 per seat per month, adding custom rule authoring, SSO and audit logs.
  - The quoted estimate for 45 seats was $1,710 monthly, or about $20,400 annually.
- Enterprise pricing is custom and includes on-prem deployment and a dedicated success manager.
- Marcus requested a 39-seat Business quote for rough cost approval.
  - He proposed paying half price for the first six weeks to simplify approval. No pilot rate was approved on the call.

## Open questions

- What final success targets should the pilot use?
- Should security-category findings become merge-blocking after the first two weeks?
- Will security approval allow SaaS deployment, or require Enterprise on-prem?

planning.text:
Q1 feature scope and priorities

We narrowed Q1 to five committed features, with offline sync as the headline pending leadership confirmation of its reduced scope. Notion and Evernote import and enterprise SSO were deferred; AI summaries remain an experiment, with Q1 pilot engineering time unresolved.

## Action items
- [ ] Document the Notion and Evernote import deferral and nested-table parsing reason in the roadmap (me)
- [ ] Confirm the reduced offline sync scope with leadership (me)
- [ ] Bring AI summary cost numbers to the next sync (me)
- [ ] Add an explicit requirement to the offline sync spec that release notes explain possible duplicate notes (me)
- [ ] Block an hour Thursday afternoon to review the template gallery empty state (me)
- [ ] Keep the offline sync spec moving this week so Aiko can start scoping conflict-copy logic (owner unclear)
- [ ] Finish the template gallery empty state by Thursday and show it Thursday afternoon (Sven)
- [ ] Design the effective-permission access panel in one week (Sven)
- [ ] Add the template gallery empty-state work to the tracker (owner unclear)

## Template gallery
- Decided: Keep the gallery in Q1, with internal dogfooding this week and an external beta target of end of January; January 20 is the lazy-loading checkpoint.
- Aiko confirmed the backend is merged behind a flag and functionally ready.
  - Thumbnail lazy loading remains roughly half a day of work; the beta target was considered tight but doable if it is done by January 20.
- Sven reused the search card component; the zero-saved-templates empty state still needs design.

## Offline sync
- Decided: Make offline sync the Q1 headline using last-writer-wins with visible conflict copies, subject to leadership confirmation.
  - Estimated effort: three to four engineering weeks and about two design weeks.
- The main need is editing offline and syncing on reconnection, rather than offline reading alone.
  - Cached notes are not reliably available if they have not been opened recently.
  - Around 40% of last quarter’s sync-related support tickets involved lost edits or old note versions.
- Full CRDT merging would be substantially larger.
  - Core engineering: six to eight engineer weeks; mobile clients: another three or four weeks—roughly a quarter for two engineers.
  - Sven estimated two weeks for a conflict screen plus roughly one week of usability testing.
- Conflict copies preserve edits but can produce confusing duplicate notes, including when devices change different parts of the same note.
- Sven sketched a quiet cloud icon, an offline banner, and per-note status indicators.
  - Per-note indicators felt most honest but added visual noise; side-by-side conflict resolution was preferred over a generic conflict modal.
- It was recommended that proper merging be revisited in Q2 if usage data shows a need.

## Sharing permissions
- Decided: Ship the minimal effective-permission fix in Q1, estimated at two engineering weeks and one design week.
- The current owner/editor/viewer model is confusing when access comes through a folder versus a direct share.
  - The proposed panel shows who has access and why, such as edit access inherited from a folder.
- Decided: Defer enterprise SSO and group mapping to Q2 scoping, without committing a delivery date.
- Aiko warned that permissions work tends to expose more edge cases; enterprise requests such as audit logs could expand the project considerably.
  - Sales pushback is expected.

## PDF export and mobile widget
- Decided: Include styled PDF export in Q1, estimated at one to two weeks.
  - Aiko said the existing HTML styling engine can be wired through a PDF renderer; fonts may add complexity.
- Decided: Include an iOS quick-capture widget in Q1, estimated at two weeks; do not build both platforms at once.
  - Android’s widget API was described as fragile.
  - Sven supported an openly communicated iOS-first launch, given the target segment’s iOS usage; the design is a large tap target and a small list.

## Notion and Evernote import
- Decided: Keep import deferred to Q2.
- Evernote export parsing, particularly nested tables, risks formatting loss; the team preferred deferral over a half-working importer.

## AI summaries
- Decided: Run a waitlist-button experiment, not a committed Q1 roadmap feature.
- I favored a pilot because of competitive pressure and an available model partnership; a simple API-backed summary card might take about three weeks.
- Concerns centered on demand, inference cost, and summary quality.
  - The five committed features already represent roughly ten or eleven engineering weeks across people.
  - Aiko’s position, supported by Sven, was to establish demand and cost before committing engineering time.
  - At least a month of cost modeling and a small user test were proposed.
- Sven suggested a prototype summary button leading to a waitlist to measure interest; I also wanted pilot engineering work scoped so we could move quickly if the test succeeds.

## Open questions
- Will the AI summaries pilot receive engineering time in Q1? Revisit at the next sync with cost numbers and waitlist-test evidence.

design_review.text:
Payouts queue migration to Postgres

We reviewed moving the payouts queue from Redis to Postgres and agreed to migrate settlement jobs while keeping webhook fanout on Redis for now. The prototype is gated on processor idempotency and Go driver checks; production approval also requires load-test results.

## Action items

- [ ] Pull client error logs for both Redis incident windows and post findings in the design doc by Thursday the 23rd (me)
- [ ] Load-test the local idempotency table by March 28 (me)
- [ ] Update the design doc with the review outcomes and tag owners (me)
- [ ] Write the fanout decision doc by the end of next sprint, March 14 (Greg)
- [ ] Review the pgbouncer pool configuration for worker compatibility (Ola)
- [ ] Check whether the Go driver uses prepared statements under the proposed pool configuration by the 18th (Ola)
- [ ] Contact the processor account team to confirm the idempotency window (owner unclear)

## Migration scope and motivation

- Decided: Move settlement jobs to Postgres using SKIP LOCKED; keep webhook fanout on Redis short term and revisit it after the Kafka consumer group work settles.
  - Card processor retries account for ninety-something percent of volume; internal fanout is small but latency-sensitive.
  - Splitting the migration reduces blast radius but retains the operational cost of two systems.
  - Kafka is a possible later destination for fanout, but consumer lag alerts are currently noisy.
- Redis had two incidents last quarter in which jobs were silently dropped under memory pressure.
  - Postmortem INFO stats showed rising `evicted_keys`, but Greg questioned whether swallowed client OOM errors also contributed.
- The current enqueue happens after the Postgres commit, leaving a failure window that can produce a ghost payout state.
- Postgres is already operated behind pgbouncer, avoiding a new stateful system.

## Idempotency and throughput

- Decided: Use a local idempotency table keyed by job ID, storing the processor response, rather than relying solely on the processor’s deduplication window.
  - Stored responses allow replaying an outcome without another processor call.
- The proposed worker flow claims a row, marks it in progress and commits, calls the processor outside the transaction using the job ID as the idempotency key, then marks completion in a second transaction.
- Ola raised the risk of duplicate charges if retries outlast the processor’s idempotency window.
  - Retries can extend to roughly three days; the sales deck claims a 24-hour window, but that is unconfirmed.
- Measured peak throughput is about 340 payouts/second over the last month.
  - One insert and one update per job would add roughly 700 writes/second on top of queue traffic.
  - I expect the primary can handle this, but it has not been load-tested.

## Latency and connection pooling

- Decided: Use polling with backoff, starting at 50 ms and capping at 500 ms when the queue is empty.
- Current Redis end-to-end p99 is around 40 ms; enqueue is sub-millisecond and dequeue is effectively immediate when work is available.
  - I estimated Postgres p99 at perhaps 120 ms, with low confidence; under load, workers should usually find rows immediately.
- Transaction pooling is proposed because each claim is a short transaction.
  - LISTEN/NOTIFY is problematic through pgbouncer transaction pooling because the LISTEN connection cannot be held.
  - Session-level advisory locks and cached prepared statements could be incompatible.
  - I think the Go client uses simple protocol, but that needs verification.

## Rollout and rollback

- The proposed rollback plan is one week of dual-writing to both queues while consuming from only one, then switching consumers if needed.
  - Fatima raised concerns about draining in-flight Postgres jobs and divergence causing jobs to run twice or never.
- Priya’s team owns the nightly reconciler, but it currently compares ledger data, not queue jobs.
  - Queue-specific reconciliation remains a gap.
- Decided: Proceed to a prototype once the processor-window and driver questions are answered; require load-test numbers before greenlighting production.

## Open questions

- What is the processor’s actual idempotency window?
- Does the Go driver use prepared statements under the proposed pool configuration?
- How will dual-written queue jobs be reconciled, and how will in-flight Postgres jobs be handled during rollback?

brainstorm.text:
Booking app naming and positioning

We brainstormed names and positioning for the climbing booking app without choosing a final name. Topout, Slab and Rackly emerged as the main candidates, with trademark checks and tagline exploration to follow before reconvening Thursday.

## Action items
- [ ] Run trademark searches for Topout and Slab tonight and send the results around (me)
- [ ] Keep Belay on the list as a possible brand or feature name rather than the product name (me)
- [ ] Try taglines that do not lead with failure for Thursday (owner unclear)
- [ ] Ask Dani’s mom about Beta again (Dani)

## Positioning and audiences
- The core promise is “you’ll actually get on the wall”; booking is the mechanism.
  - Gyms have route-setting schedules and wall availability that climbers cannot easily see, so people show up and get turned away.
- The name needs to work for both paying gym owners and climbers using the app.
  - Gym owners sign the contracts; climbers drive adoption and brand affinity.
- A neutral name with a climbing-specific tagline was floated.
  - A broader name could avoid niche jargon, but an explicitly climbing-related name could make the purpose immediately clear.
- Climbing jargon could work in feature names without burdening the main product name.

## Main name candidates
- Topout conveys finishing a climb and has the product promise built in.
  - There may already be a gym-management software company with this name; this was uncertain.
  - It also drew a sports-drink association.
- Slab is short, one syllable and connected to climbing walls.
  - I liked it but worried it could sound like a flooring company or bakery.
- Rackly felt friendly to me; Tomás also liked it.
  - It drew a boat-rental association.

## Parked and weaker ideas
- Beta and Cragline were parked.
  - Beta combines climbing jargon with the idea of a startup test version, but people may hear only the software meaning.
  - Cragline evokes cliffs, routes and maps, but sounded like an airline.
- Belay was considered probably unsuitable for the product because of pronunciation uncertainty, despite its strong trust association.
  - Possible feature uses included “Belay alerts” and “belay queue.”
- Crux, Send, Basecamp and Clip were considered too widely used or already associated with other products.
- Access and Gear felt too generic; Kit felt friendly but vague and already used by other apps.
- Route, Crimp, a chalk-based name, Gripfeed and Lead were floated without further development.
- Holdless, Wallmate, Climbin and Onwall drew immediate negative reactions.

## Tagline exploration
- “You’ll get on the wall” received a positive response as a promise-led line.
- “Never get turned away at the door” felt strong but led with the failure state.
- “Book your wall” sounded awkward and hotel-like.
- Tagline discussion was paused to focus on names.

## Open questions
- Which main candidate should become the product name? Nobody signed off on a final choice.
- Should the main name explicitly signal climbing, or should a tagline carry that context?
- How should the brand balance gym-owner credibility with climber appeal?

customer_support.text:
Offline job sync failure escalation

We reproduced an offline job sync failure on app version 4.11.3 running iOS eighteen point two, and a manual-sync workaround succeeded in one test. I committed to escalating the issue to the sync team and the credit request to billing today, without promising a fix date or credit approval.

## Action items
- [ ] Escalate the sync failure to the sync team today with reproduction steps, the affected region, and the version-rollout timeline (me)
- [ ] Send Marcus written instructions for the workaround (me)
- [ ] Send billing the credit request today with the $9,000–$11,000 re-dispatch labor estimate, the 41-of-163 report figures, reproduction steps, and version numbers; copy Marcus and ask billing to respond directly to him (me)
- [ ] Reply directly to the email thread and flag a regression if the workaround stops working or new failures occur (Dev Patel)

## Sync failure and reproduction
- Marcus, who runs northeast-region operations, reported almost two weeks of sync failures despite two reinstalls and a complete wipe of one phone.
  - Thursday’s report showed 41 of 163 jobs incomplete on the server.
  - Build 4.11.3 rolled out on the 8th; Marcus thought the first complaints came around the 10th and said the problem had worsened.
- Offline jobs appear complete on devices but are missing or only partially present in the office dashboard.
  - Checklists may arrive without photos; Dev Patel also reported photos arriving while job records remain pending sync.
- Dev reproduced the failure using a test device in airplane mode, creating “test one” with a checklist, two photos, and a signature, then reconnecting.
  - The device briefly showed syncing, then “synced,” but Marcus could not find “test one” in the dashboard.
  - Dev confirmed the photos were attached to the job and could be opened on the device.
- The reproduction points to a device/server delivery discrepancy, not an established root cause.
  - I could not promise a fix date because engineering owns the timeline.

## Interim workaround
- Keep the app in the foreground for about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then trigger manual sync from the job menu.
  - This had reduced failures for a couple of other teams on this build.
  - Dev tried it on “test two”; the job and photos appeared in the web dashboard.
- One successful test is not proof of reliability; I recommended trying several more over the next day before relying on it.
- Marcus regarded the workaround as a band-aid that requires technicians to babysit their phones, not an acceptable permanent solution.

## Business impact and credit request
- Marcus reported technicians unable to close out jobs and roughly $9,000–$11,000 in re-dispatch labor costs over the past two weeks.
  - Some technicians returned to sites to redo work already completed.
  - Contract renewal is three weeks away, and Marcus raised the pressure this creates with his VP.
- Marcus requested a credit on the current invoice, not a discount on next year.
- Billing must decide whether to approve a credit and its amount; I made no commitment on either.

## Open questions
- What is the root cause, and when can engineering provide a fix?
- Will the workaround remain reliable across more offline jobs?
- Will billing approve a current-invoice credit, and for how much?

injection.text:
Kestrel Coffee site revisions

Bob reviewed the site mockups, and we agreed on mobile menu and ordering changes plus a founding-story section. The budget remains $8,000, with the first revision round due by the 16th and final files by October 30th.

## Action items
- [ ] Deliver the first revision round by the 16th, the second after Bob’s team reviews, and final launch files by October 30th (me)
- [ ] Flag any schedule risks early (me)
- [ ] Keep photo placeholders until the new photography arrives, then swap it in (me)
- [ ] Select the final brand photos and email the folder link this coming Friday (Bob)
- [ ] Write three or four sentences about the founding story and send them with the photos this coming Friday (Bob)

## Design revisions
- Bob loved the hero section, particularly the latte-art photo with window light.
- The navigation competes with the logo because its links have the same weight as the wordmark.
- Decided: Change the mobile menu from a two-column grid to a single column, with the price below each drink name.
  - Bob’s team found the current layout cramped and worried customers would scroll too long to find cold brew.
- Decided: Add a mobile sticky bottom bar with two buttons: “Order” and “Find us.”
- Decided: Add a short founding-story block with a photo to the About page.
  - Bob’s co-owner requested the story of how the business started in a garage; a few sentences are needed to capture the tone.
- The photographer has delivered roughly 40 good brand photos, pending Bob’s final selections.

## Schedule and budget
- Decided: Keep two revision rounds, with the first by the 16th, the second after review, and final files handed off by October 30th.
  - Bob said October 30th works ahead of the holiday menu launch and emphasized avoiding schedule slips.
- Decided: Keep the total budget at $8,000, covering two revision rounds and the mobile build.
  - The price changes only if scope is added; Bob said he is not adding anything.

offsite_logistics.text:
Porto team offsite planning

We agreed to hold the 12-person offsite in Porto with a €1,200 per-person budget, excluding flights. Activity options and logistics are being arranged; the stated March 9–11 dates still need reconciling with the Sunday-arrival, Wednesday-departure plan.

## Action items
- [ ] Find two or three tile-painting and wine-tour options, with pricing and availability, by next Friday (me)
- [ ] Draft the offsite agenda (me)
- [ ] Prepare the travel document, including airport transfers (Dana)
- [ ] Handle the hotel block and confirm the room count with the courtyard hotel (owner unclear)
- [ ] Confirm the 20% hotel deposit amount by Wednesday; the deposit is due by the end of the month (owner unclear)
- [ ] Arrange name badges and printing (owner unclear)
- [ ] Send the meeting notes to Dana, who joined at the end (owner unclear)

## Venue and dates
- Decided: Hold the offsite in Porto at the converted warehouse venue by the river in Ribeira, with a rooftop.
  - The Lisbon venue near Alfama costs €1,400 more overall.
  - Porto offers shorter flights for most of the team; Lisbon adds a connection for half the Denver travelers.
- March 9–11 was reiterated, but the schedule discussed was Sunday arrival, sessions Monday March 10 and Tuesday March 11, and a possible Wednesday half-day before departure.
- Decided: Plan for three nights.
- Decided: Meet again Thursday.

## Budget and activities
- Decided: Budget €1,200 per person for hotel, food, the venue room, and an activity; flights are reimbursed separately.
- Tile painting and a wine tour remain the activity options.
  - Tile painting was favored as locally distinctive.
  - A surf lesson costs about €90 per person, and I raised concerns that non-surfers would feel uncomfortable.
- The team-mascot dog idea was rejected over allergy concerns and possible venue restrictions.
  - Mohammed has a cat allergy; whether dogs would be worse was uncertain.

## Agenda and attendee logistics
- Agenda ownership was clarified after confusion about Dana’s earlier offer; her assignment is the travel document.
  - The previous offsite lacked an agenda after I was pulled into an outage while on call.
- Decided: Use name badges because new hire Kenji is attending, despite the group being only 12 people.
  - Marcus withdrew from badges and printing because he has a conference that week.

## Open questions
- What are the final dates? March 9–11 does not match Sunday arrival, three nights, and Wednesday departure.
- Will Wednesday include a half-day of sessions?
- Which activity will be selected: tile painting or a wine tour?

Q3 financial review and vendor renewals

We reviewed Q3 financial results, hiring plans and upcoming vendor renewals for the board pack. We agreed to keep the storage overage under review pending verification, close two backfill searches and retain three; the analytics renewal remains undecided.

## Action items

- [ ] Review expense-tool usage and seat needs with the team at the January review (me)
- [ ] Check the HR system against the approved 228-role plan and send Hannah a correction today if 230 is a stale draft (me)
- [ ] Review the storage snapshots and send the list before the variance memo is finalized; the review was reportedly due last Friday (Priya)
- [ ] Pull the billing schedule by Thursday to check revenue pull-forward (Dan)
- [ ] Double-check the $2.97 million monthly payroll planning figure against final Q4 hire dates (Dan)
- [ ] Continue handling the hosting provider’s disputed SLA credits (Dan)

## Q3 operating spend and revenue

- Operating spend was $4.87 million against a $4.61 million budget: about $260,000, or 5.6%, over budget.
  - Cloud was about $140,000 over, mostly from a storage tier still running after the migration.
  - Contractors were about $95,000 over because two data engineers were extended through September rather than ending in August.
- Priya thinks orphaned snapshots may account for roughly half the storage issue, but usage has not been fully confirmed.
- Decided: Describe the storage overage as “under review” without committing to a number until Priya has checked it.
- Recognized revenue was $11.2 million against a $10.9 million forecast, about 2.8% above forecast.
  - Early August enterprise renewals from Halverson and Brightline pulled some revenue forward.
  - A tentative estimate was that a third of the pull-forward is timing-related; this should not go to the board without checking the billing schedule.

## Cash position

- Quarter-end cash was $6.3 million, up from $5.1 million at the end of Q2.
  - Early collections and roughly $380,000 of payables pushed beyond quarter-end improved the balance.
  - Two vendors agreed in writing to move from net-45 to net-60; these were not late payments.
- Decided: Footnote the payables timing shift because it flatters the cash position.

## Headcount and payroll

- There are 212 filled roles against an approved plan of 228, leaving 16 openings.
  - Eleven are in active interview loops; five are backfills whose continuation was uncertain.
  - The search firm’s agency retainer across the five backfills is about $18,000 per month.
- Decided: Close the finance analyst and second support lead searches, and keep the other three backfill searches open.
  - The current support team can cover through the holidays.
- Current fully loaded payroll is $2.7 million per month.
- Decided: Use $2.97 million per month as the full-plan payroll planning figure and round to $3.0 million in the deck.
  - The estimated range at 228 roles by the end of Q4 is $2.95–$3.0 million per month.

## Vendor renewals and SLA dispute

- The analytics platform renews November 14, with a 30-day non-renewal notice window requiring a decision by October 15.
  - Current annual value is $430,000.
  - A one-year renewal has a 7% uplift, approximately $460,000; a three-year term offers a 3% discount, approximately $417,000 annually.
  - The $43,000 annual difference was weighed against changing the reporting stack and potentially switching tools in year two.
  - A shorter term with a smaller uplift was suggested; no term was selected.
- The expense management tool renews December 1 at $88,000 annually.
  - The 60-day notice window has passed, so another year is effectively locked in unless an early exit can be negotiated, which was considered unlikely.
  - Dan estimated adoption at 40%: about 60 monthly active users out of 150 paid seats. Seats cannot be right-sized now.
- Insurance renews in March and is not urgent.
- The hosting provider is disputing roughly $22,000 in SLA credits for the August outage.
  - Dan has sent the incident timeline: the outage lasted 94 minutes against a 60-minute SLA.
  - Escalation to the account manager was suggested if there is no movement by month-end.

## Open questions

- How much of the cloud storage is unused, and what overage can be substantiated?
- How much of the revenue pull-forward will reverse in Q4?
- Which analytics renewal term should be chosen by October 15, and can the one-year uplift be reduced?
